# FPT-Approximability of Stable Matching Problems

**Abstract**

We study parameterized approximability of three optimization problems related to stable matching: (1) Min-BP-SMI: Given a stable marriage instance and a number _k_, find a size-at-least-_k_ matching that minimizes the number \(\beta\) of blocking pairs; (2) Min-BP-SRI: Given a stable roommates instance, find a matching that minimizes the number \(\beta\) of blocking pairs; (3) Max-SMTI: Given a stable marriage instance with preferences containing ties, find a maximum-size stable matching.

The first two problems are known to be NP-hard to approximate to any constant factor and W[1]- hard with respect to \(\beta\), making the existence of an EPTAS or FPT-algorithms unlikely. We show that they are W[1]-hard with respect to \(\beta\) to approximate to any function of \(\beta\). This means that unless FPT=W[1], there is no FPT-algorithm with respect to \(\beta\) that can decide whether a given instance has a matching with at most \(\beta\) or at least \(F(\beta)\) blocking pairs for every function _F_ depending only on \(\beta\). The last problem (Max-SMTI) is known to be NP-hard to approximate to factor-\(\frac{29}{33}\) and W[1]-hard with respect to the number of ties. We complement this and present an FPT-approximation scheme for the parameter "number of agents with ties".

### 1 Introduction

Stable matchings play a fundamental role in various applications ranging from job markets (e.g., the National Resident Matching Program), over education (e.g., school choice or college admission), to health (e.g., kidney exchange programs). The general idea is to match the agents into pairs so no two agents can form a blocking pair. A blocking pair is a pair of two agents that are not matched with each other but prefer each other over the status under the matching.

In the classical Stable Marriage (SM) problem introduced by Gale and Shapley [11], we are given two disjoint sets of agents, each having a complete and strict preference list (aka. ranking) over the agents of the other set, and we aim to match every agent from one set to an agent of the other set so that no blocking pairs are induced. Gale and Shapley show that every instance of the SM problem admits a stable matching and provide a linear-time algorithm to find one.

SM has many relevant extensions. First, the preference lists of the agents may be _incomplete_, allowing them to express unacceptability towards other agents. This results in the setting of Stable Marriage with Incomplete Preferences (SMI). A stable matching still always exists for each SMI instance, albeit not every agent is matched; the same set of agents are matched in all stable matchings though. A key challenge in SMI is the trade-off between the size and stability: Requiring more agents to be matched will induce blocking pairs, destroying stability [26, Rural Hospital Theorem]. This motivates the problem of Minimum Blocking Pairs SMI which aims to find a matching of size at least a given number _k_ such that the number of blocking pairs is minimized. Prior work has considered both exact and approximation algorithms [3, 14, 12], showing that the problem remains computationally challenging. For instance, Min- BP-SMI is already NP-hard when the preference lists are of length at most three [3]. Moreover, it is NP-hard to approximate to some constant factor [3, 14].

Another extension of SM is to have just one set of agents, allowing each agent to rank any other agent. In this case, we obtain the setting of Stable Roommates (SR). Unlike in SM and SMI, stable matchings are not guaranteed to exist. Irving [17] designs a linear-time algorithm to decide whether a given

To deal with the non-existence of stable matching, Biró et al. \[4\] introduce the problem of finding a matching that minimizes the number of blocking pairs, called Min- BP-SRI. Unfortunately, Min-BP-SRI is W\[1\]-hard with respect to the number \(\beta\) of blocking pairs \[6\] and NP-hard to approximate \[4\].

A third variant of SM is to allow agents to have both _incomplete_ and _indifferent_ preferences and between agents. In this case, a stable matching<sup>1</sup> still exists, but different stable matchings may have different sizes. A commonly studied goal for incomplete preferences with ties is to find a stable matching with maximum size. This gives rise to the setting of Maximum-Size Stable Marriage with Incomplete preferences and Ties (Max-SMTI). Max-SMTI is NP-hard to approximate \[22\] and W\[1\]-hard with respect to the number of ties \[24\].

The above inapproximability and parameterized intractability results beg the study of approximation algorithms combined with fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) algorithms. Given the inherent computational hardness of Min-BP-SMI, Min-BP-SRI, and Max-SMTI, parameterized complexity provides a natural framework to explore efficient algorithms when certain problem parameters are small. In this work, we investigate FPT-approximability for both minimizing the number of blocking pairs and maximizing the size of stable matchings in presence of ties.

## 1.1 Our Contributions

We show that Min-BP-SMI and Min-BP-SRI remain resistant to FPT-approximability. More precisely, both problems are W\[1\]-hard with respect to \(\beta\) to approximate to a factor \(F(\beta)\cdot n^{O(1)}\), where _n_ is the number of agents, \(\beta\) is the number of blocking pairs, _F_ is an arbitrary computable function. In other words, it is unlikely to obtain an FPT algorithm with respect to \(\beta\) that can distinguish between instances that have at most \(\beta\) or at least \(F(\beta)\) blocking pairs. This hardness result for Min-BP-SMI holds even when we require the matching to be perfect, i.e., every agent has to be matched. On the other hand, when preferences can be incomplete and may have ties, we provide a simple FPT-approximation scheme for Max-SMTI with respect to the number \(\tau\) of agents with ties, i.e., an approximation scheme that given an instance _I_ of SMTI, where \(\tau\) agents have preferences containing ties, and an approximation ratio \(\varepsilon\), outputs in \(f(\varepsilon,\tau)\cdot|I|^{O(1)}\) time a stable matching with size at least \(\varepsilon\cdot\text{OPT}(I)\), where OPT(_I_) denotes the size of a largest stable matching in _I_ and _f_ is a computable function depending only on \(\varepsilon\) and \(\tau\).

## 1.2 Related Work

Min-BP-SMI and Min-BP-SRI are particularly difficult to approximate. Biró et al. \[3\] and Hamada et al. \[14\] show that Min-BP-SMI is NP-hard to approximate to factor \(n^{1-\varepsilon}\) for any \(\varepsilon>0\), where _n_ is the number of agents. The result holds even when the desired matching size is \(k=\frac{n}{2}\) , i.e., every agent has to be matched. Hamada et al. \[15\] extend the result to the Hospital-Residents problem. Biró et al. \[3\] show that Min- BP-SMI remains NP-hard to approximate to some constant factor \(\delta>1\), even when the preference lists are of length at most three. On the positive side, when one side of the preference lists have length at most two, Min-BP-SMI becomes polynomial-time solvable. For the roommates setting, Biró et al. \[4\] show that Min-BP-SRI is NP-hard to approximate to factor \(n^\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon\) for any \(\varepsilon>0\). They also consider the case when the preference lists have length at most _d_. They obtain a dichotomy result: The problem remains NP-hard to approximate to some constant factor even when _d_=3, but can be approximated within factor 2_d_-3 in general. If \(d\le 2\), then the problem becomes polynomial-time solvable.

The parameterized complexity of the canonical decision variants of Min-BP-SMI and Min-BP-SRI has attracted some study; in what follows we use Min-BP-SMI and Min-BP-SRI to refer to the decision variants for the sake of brevity. Gupta et al. \[12\] show that Min-BP-SMI remains W\[1\]-hard for the combined parameter \(\beta+t+d\), where \(\beta\) is the number of blocking pairs, _t_ the increase in size to a stable matching of the instance, and _d_ the maximum length of a preference list. Towards tractability, they present an algorithm for a local search variant of the problem. More precisely, they provide an FPT-algorithm for finding a matching<tbc>

<sup>1</sup>When preferences have ties, our definition of stability is also known as weak stability, distinguishing it from the case of strong stability or super stability \[21\]. For strong stability, for each pair of agents _at least one_ agent in the pair must prefer his partner over the other agent in the pair. For super stability, for each pair of agents _each agent_ in the pair must prefer his partner over the other agent in the pair.

<tbc>that differs from a given matching \(\mu\) by at most _q_ edges, has at most _k_ blocking pairs, and has size at least \(|\mu|+t\), parameterized by _q+k+t_. Moreover, they show that this local search problem is W\[1\]-hard parameterized by _k+t_ even when the maximum length of a preference list is three. Chen et al. \[6\] study the parameterized complexity of two optimization variants of SRI and SRTI (Stable Roommates with Ties and Incomplete lists), one being Min-BP-SRI and the other Egalitarian SR, which aims at a stable matching with minimum egalitarian cost (i.e., sum of the ranks of the agents’ partners). They show that Min-BP-SRI-dec is W\[1\]-hard with respect to \(\beta\), even when the preference lists are of length at most five. Abraham et al. \[1\] show that Min-BP-SRI is XP with respect to \(\beta\), i.e., it is solvable in polynomial time for every fixed constant \(\beta\).

Now we turn to the last problem Max-SMTI. Manlove et al. \[22\] show that Max-SMTI is NP-hard. Irving et al. \[18\] strengthen this by showing that the hardness remains even when one side has preference lists of length at most three. From the approximation point of view, Király \[19\] and McDermid \[25\] show that Max-SMTI can be approximated to factor \(\frac{2}{3}\). Yanagisawa \[28\] show the problem does not admit a factor-\(\frac{29}{33}\) approximation (polynomial-time) algorithm unless P=NP. Dudycz et al. \[9\] and Huang et al. \[16\] show that under the assumption of one of two different variants of Unique Games Conjecture, the factor-\(\frac{2}{3}\) approximation algorithm by Király \[19\] and McDermid \[25\] are that best achievable ones. Further approximation results for Max-SMTI under various restrictions have been presented, see for example \[16, 7, 20\].

Marx and Schlotter \[24\], Adil et al. \[2\] investigate parameterized complexity of Max-SMTI. Marx and Schlotter \[24\] show that Max-SMTI is W\[1\]-hard with respect to the number of ties, but FPT with respect to the total sum of the lengths of the ties. They also study fixed-parameter tractability of other variants of SMTI, such as egalitarian and minimum regret SMTI. Adil et al. \[2\] show that Max-SMTI admits a size-_O(k_<sup>2</sup>) problem kernel and can be solved in _k_<sup>_O(k_)</sup>+_n_<sup>_O_(1)</sup> time.

Parameterized approximation has also been studied in the context of voting. Bredereck et al. \[5\] show that Minimum Cost Borda Shift Bribery admits an FPT-approximation scheme for the parameter number of shifts. Skowron and Faliszewski \[27\] and Gupta et al. \[13\] study the fixed-parameter approximability of multiwinner voting rules.

## 2 Preliminaries

Given a non-negative integer _t_, we use \[_t_\] to denote the set {1_,...,t_}.

### Preference profiles and stable matchings.

Let _V_ be a set of _n_ agents with _V_={_v_<sub>1</sub>_,...,v<sub>n</sub>_}. Each agent \(v_i\in V\) has a subset \(V_i\subseteq V\backslash\{i\}\) that it finds _acceptable_ and has a _preference list_ \(\unknown_i\) on _V<sub>i</sub>_ which is a weak order over _V<sub>i</sub>_. We assume the acceptability to be mutualm, i.e., an agent _x_ is in the preference list of another agent _y_ if and only _y_ is also in the preference list of _x_. For two acceptable agents \(x,y\in V_i\) of _v<sub>i</sub>_, we say that _v<sub>i</sub> weakly prefers x_ over _y_ if \(x\unknown_iy\). If not also \(y\unknown_ix\), we write \(x\succ y\) and say that _v<sub>i</sub> strictly prefers_ (or simply _prefers_) _x_ over _y_. If \(x\unknown_iy\) and \(y\unknown_x\), we write _x∼<sub>i</sub>y_, and say that _v<sub>i</sub>_ is _indifferent_ between _x_ and _y_, and has _ties_ in his preference list.

A preference profile \(\mathcal{P}=(V,(\unknown_i)_{i\in V})\) is a collection of the agents and their preference lists. Associated to each preference profile P there is an underlying _acceptability graph G_, which has _V_ as its vertex set, and an edge between each pair of agents who find each other acceptable. We say that P is a _marriage_ instance if the corresponding acceptability graph is bipartite, otherwise it is a _roommates_ instance. Further, P is _complete_ if the acceptability graph is complete.

We say that P contains _ties_ if there is an agent \(v_i\in V\) and two other agents \(x,y\in V_i\) such that _x∼<sub>i</sub>y_. If P has no ties, then we say that it is _strict_.

For example, assume we have four agents {_v_<sub>1</sub>_,v_<sub>2</sub>_,v_<sub>3</sub>_,v_<sub>4</sub>}. Let agent _v_<sub>1</sub>’s preference list be \(v_2\succ_1v_3\sim_1v_4\). This means that agent _v_<sub>1</sub> prefers _v_<sub>2</sub> to both _v_<sub>3</sub> and _v_<sub>4</sub>, but is indifferent between _v_<sub>3</sub> and _v_<sub>4</sub>.

The _rank_ of an agent _x_ in the preference list of another agent _v<sub>i</sub>_ denotes the number of agents that _v<sub>i</sub>_ strictly prefers over _x_: \(\mathrm{rank}_i^\mathcal{P}(x):=|\{y\in V_i|y\succ_ix\}|\). We omit the superscript P if it is clear from the context.

Given a preference profile \(\mathcal{P}=(V,(\unknown_i)_{i\in V})\), a _matching_ \(M\subseteq E(G)\) is a subset of disjoint edges in _G_. Given an pair \(\{v_i,v_j\}\in M\), we say that _v<sub>j</sub>_ is the _partner_ of _v<sub>i</sub>_, denoted _M(v<sub>i</sub>_), and we say that _v<sub>i</sub>_ and<tbc>

_vj_ are _matched_. If there is no pair \(e\in M\) such that \(v_i\in e\), then we say that _vi_ is _unmatched_, denoted as \(M(v_i)=\perp\). We assume that every agent _vi_ prefers to be matched with an acceptable agent over being unmatched \(\perp\). Given a matching _M_ of P, a pair \(\{v_i,v_j\}\in E(G)\) of agents is a _blocking_ pair of and _blocks M_ if \(\{v_i,v_j\}\notin M\) and the following two conditions hold: (i) _vi_ is unmatched or prefers _vj_ to _M(vi_), and (ii) _vj_ is unmatched or prefers _vi_ to _M(vj_). We call a matching _M stable_ if there is no blocking pair; otherwise we call it _unstable_. If every agent is matched, then we call the matching _perfect_. ## Problem definitions. We are ready to formally define the computational problems studied in this paper. Minimum Blocking Pairs SMI (in short Min-BP-SMI)
**Input:** A marriage instance \(\mathcal{P}=(U\cup W,(\unknown_i)_{i\in U\cup W})\) with strict preferences and a non-negative integer _k_.
**Task:** Find a matching _M_ of size \(|M|\ge k\) with minimum number of blocking pairs. Minimum Blocking Pairs SRI (in short Min-BP-SRI)
**Input:** A roommates instance \(\mathcal{P}=(V,(\unknown_i)_{i\in V})\) with strict preferences.
**Task:** Find a matching with minimum number of blocking pairs. The standard parameterized decision variants of Min-BP-SMI and Min-BP-SRI, called Min-BP-SMI- dec and Min-BP-SRI-dec, additionally have as input a number \(\beta\), and asks whether there exists a solution with at most \(\beta\) blocking pairs. Now, we turn to preferences with ties. Maximum Size-SMTI (in shortMax-SMTI)
**Input:** A marriage instance \(\mathcal{P}=(U\cup W,(\unknown_i)_{i\in U\cup W})\) with incomplete preferences possibly containing ties. **Task:** Find a stable matching _M_ with maximum size. The parameterized decision variant of Max-SMTI, called Max-SMTI-dec, has an additional parameter _k_ in the input and asks whether there exists a stable matching of size at least _k_. For more details on algorithmic complexity of stable matching problems, we refer to the textbook by Manlove \[21\]. ## Fixed-parameter approximability. We assume basic knowledge of parameterized complexity and refer the textbook by Cygan et al. \[8\] for more details. The definitions for fixed-parameter approximability are based on the definitions by Marx \[23\]. We define an _optimization problem_ as a 4-tuple \((\Pi,\mathrm{sol},\mathrm{cost},\mathrm{goal})\), where - \(\Pi\) is a set of instances, - sol is a function that assigns to each instance _I_ a set consisting of all feasible solutions, i.e., for each \(I\in\Pi\), sol(_I_) is a collection of feasible solutions, - cost is a function that assigns to each instance _I_ and each feasible solution \(x\in\mathrm{sol}(I)\) an integer that describes the quality of the solution, - goal is min for minimization problems and max for maximization problems. For instance, for the Min-BP-SMI problem, \(\Pi\) consists of all tuples _I_=(P_,k_) such that P is a marriage instance with strict preferences, _k_ is a non-negative integer, sol(_I_) consists of all matchings of size at least _k_, cost(_M,I_) is the number of blocking pairs in _M_, and goal=min. **Definition 1** (Polynomial-time approximation algorithms)**.** To define approximation algorithms, let us first consider minimization problems. Let \((\Pi,\mathrm{sol},\mathrm{cost},\mathrm{goal})\) be a minimization problem and _I_ an instance of \(\Pi\). For a given constant \(\rho\ge 1\), we say that an algorithm _A_ is a _factor-_\(\rho\) _approximation algorithm_ for \((\Pi,\mathrm{sol},\mathrm{cost},\mathrm{goal})\) if it outputs a solution _x_ with \(\mathrm{cost}(x,I)\le\rho\cdot\mathrm{OPT}\), where OPT(_I_) is the cost of an optimal solution of _I_, i.e., \(\mathrm{OPT}(I)=\mathrm{argmin}_{x\in\mathrm{sol}}\mathrm{cost}(x,I)\). If \((\Pi,\mathrm{sol},\mathrm{cost},\mathrm{goal})\) is a maximization problem instead, then we require

\(\mathrm{cost}(x,I)\ge\rho\cdot\mathrm{OPT}(I)\) to holds for a given \(\rho\le 1\). We say that \((\Pi,\mathrm{sol},\mathrm{cost},\mathrm{goal})\) is _polynomial-time approximable_ to a factor of \(\rho\) if it admits a factor-\(\rho\) approximation algorithm that runs in polynomial time.

We say that \((\Pi,\mathrm{sol},\mathrm{cost},\mathrm{goal})\) admits a _polynomial-time approximation scheme_ (PTAS) if for every approximation error \(\varepsilon>0\), it is polynomial-time approximable to a factor of \(1+\varepsilon\) (for minimization) and \(1-\varepsilon\) (for maximization).

**Definition 2** (Fixed-parameter approximation algorithms)**.** Let \((\Pi,\mathrm{sol},\mathrm{cost},\mathrm{goal})\) be an optimization problem and _I_ an instance of \(\Pi\). We say that \((\Pi,\mathrm{sol},\mathrm{cost},\mathrm{goal})\) is FPT_-approximable to factor_ \(\rho\) with respect to a parameter _k_ if it admits a factor-\(\rho\) approximation algorithm that runs in time \(f(\rho,k)\cdot n^{O(1)}\), where _f_ is a computable function on _k_ and \(\rho\).

Consequently, we say that \((\Pi,\mathrm{sol},\mathrm{cost},\mathrm{goal})\) admits an FPT_-approximation scheme_ (FPT-AS) with respect to a parameter _k_ if for every \(\varepsilon>0\) it is FPT-approximable to factor \((1+\varepsilon)\) (for minimization) and \((1-\varepsilon)\) (for maximization) with respect to _k_.

To show that no FPT-approximation scheme exists, we need a specific reduction, called _gap-producing parameterized reduction_ \[10\]. The idea is to provide a parameterized reduction to a gap version of an optimization problem. Below, we only define the reduction for minimization problems. The one for maximization problems is analogous.

**Definition 3** (gap-producing parameterized reduction)**.** Let \(X=(\Pi,\mathrm{sol},\mathrm{cost},\mathrm{goal})\) be a minimization problem and let _k_ be the natural parameter of _X_ to turn it into a decision problem. Let \(\alpha:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{N}\) be a computable function.

A reduction _R_ from a parameterized problem \(\hat{\Pi}\) with parameter _h_ to our optimization problem _X_ parameterized by _k_ is called an \(\alpha\)_-gap producing parameterized reduction_ if for every instance \(\hat{I}\) of \(\hat{\Pi}\) with parameter _h_, _R_ produces in \(f(h)\cdot|\hat{I}|^{O(1)}\) time an instance _I_ of \(\Pi\) with parameter _k_ such that

(i) _k_ is bounded by a function of _h_,<tbc>

(ii) if \((\hat{I},h)\) is a yes-instance, then _I_ admits a solution _x_ with \(\mathrm{cost}(x,I)\le k\);<tbc>

(iii) if \((\hat{I},h)\) is a no-instance, then every solution _x_ of _I_ has \(\mathrm{cost}(x,I)>\alpha(k)\cdot k\).

The existence of an \(\alpha\)-gap-producing parameterized reduction from a parameterized intractable (e.g., W\[1\]-hard) problem shows that a factor-\(\alpha\) FPT approximation algorithm is unlikely, unless FPT=W\[1\].

## 3 FPT Inapproximability of Min-BP-SMI and Min-BP-SRI

In this section, we show that Min-BP-SMI and Min-BP-SRI remain parameterized inapproximable with respect to \(\beta\), where \(\beta\) denotes the number of blocking pairs in the natural parameterization variant of the problems. The idea is to present a gap producing reduction from the Clique problem that is W\[1\]-hard with respect to the size _h_ of clique.

Clique

**Input:** A directed graph _G_=(_V,E_) and a non-negative number _h_.

**Question:** Does _G_ admit a _clique_ \(K\subseteq V\) of size at least _h_, , i.e., _G_\[_K_\] is a complete subgraph (aka. _clique_) of size at least _h_?

We remark that the reduction presented here is a modified version of Theorem 1 by Gupta et al. \[12\]. In their reduction, the vertex gadget is connected to the edge gadget by an edge. However, we add \([(h+\genfrac(){pt}{2}{h}{2})\cdot F(h+\genfrac(){pt}{2}{h}{2})+1]\) cycles of length four to connect a vertex gadget with an "incident" edge gadget instead to boost the gap.

**Theorem 1.** _Let_ \(F:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{N}\) _be an arbitrary computable function. Given an instance_ \((\mathcal{P},k,\beta)\) _of_ Min-BP- SMI-dec _it is_ W\[1\]_-hard to distinguish between the following two cases:_

(_i)_ P _admits a size-k matching with at most_ \(\beta\) _blocking pairs._<tbc>

_(ii)_ _Every size-at-least k matching of_ P _has at least_ \(F(\beta)\cdot\beta\) _blocking pairs._

_Proof._ We reduce from Clique, parameterized by the clique size _h_. Let (_G_=(_V,E),h_) be an instance of Clique with \(V=\{v_1,\dots v_\hat{n}\}\) and \(E=\{e_1,\dots,e_{\hat{m}}\}\). We construct an instance (_I,k_) of Min-BP-SMI as follows; the construction is illustrated in Figure 1. For brevity’s sake, define \(L:=(h+\genfrac(){pt}{2}{h}{2})\cdot F(h+\genfrac(){pt}{2}{h}{2})+1\).

## Agents. We create two disjoint sets of agents, _U_ and _W_. - For every \(z\in[h]\), we create two vertex selector agents _sz_ and _tz_, and add them to _U_ and _W_, respectively. - For every \(p\in[\genfrac(){pt}{2}{h}{2}]\), we create two edge selector agents \(\hat{s}_p\) and \(\hat{t}_p\), and add them to _U_ and _W_, respectively. **-** For every vertex \(v_i\in V\) , we create four vertex-agents _ui_, \(\hat{u}_i\), _wi_, and \(\hat{w}_i\), and add the first two to _U_, and the last two to _W_. **-** For every edge \(e\in E\), we do the following. We create two edge-agents _xe_ and _ye_, and add them to _U_ and _W_, respectively. Additionally, let _vi_ and _vj_ denote the two endpoints of _e_, then, we create 8 groups of edge agents \(\pi_e^{u_i}[r]\), \(1\pi_e^{u_j}[r]\), \(\hat{\pi}_e^{u_i}[r]\), \(\hat{\pi}_e^{u_j}[r]\), \(\theta_e^{u_i}[r]\), \(\theta_e^{u_j}[r]\), \(\hat{\theta}_e^{u_i}[r]\), \(\hat{\theta}_e^{u_j}[r]\), for \(r\in[L]\). We add the first four groups to _U_ and the last four groups to _W_. Note that these edge agents’ preference orders will enforce that matching two adjacent vertices to the selector agents will induce too many blocking pairs (at least _L_). Summarizing, \(U:=\{s_z|z\in[h]\}\cup\{\hat{s}_p|p\in[\genfrac(){pt}{2}{h}{2}]\}\cup\{u_i,\hat{u}_i|v_i\in V\}\cup\{x_e|e\in E\}\cup\{\pi_e^{u_i}[r],\pi_e^{u_j}[r],\hat{\pi}_e^{u_i}[r],\hat{\pi}_e^{u_i}[r]|e\in E\) with \(e=\{v_i,v_j\},r\in[L]\}\) and \(W:=\{t_z|z\in[h]\}\cup\{\hat{t}_p|p\in[\genfrac(){pt}{2}{h}{2}]\}\cup\{w_i,\hat{w}_i|v_i\in V\}\cup\{y_e|e\in E\}\cup\{\theta_e^{u_i}[r],\theta_e^{u_j}[r],\hat{\theta}_e^{u_i}[r],\hat{\theta}_e^{u_j}[r]|e\in E\) with \(e=\{v_i,v_j\},r\in[L]\}\). In total, we have created \(2(h+\genfrac(){pt}{2}{h}{2}+2\hat{n}+\hat{m}+4\hat{m}\cdot L)\) agents. ## Agents’ preference orders. For a given subset _Q_ of agents, let \(\langle Q\rangle\) denote an arbitrary but fixed linear order of the elements in _Q_. The preference orders of the agents are as follows, where \(z\in[h]\), \(p\in[\genfrac(){pt}{2}{h}{2}]\), \(r\in[L]\), \(e\in E\) with _e_={_vi,vj_}, \(\Theta(v_i):=\{\theta_{e^\prime}^{u_i}[r']|v_i\in e'\) for some \(e'\in E\wedge r'\in[L]\}\), and \(\Pi(e):=\{\pi_e^{u_i}[r'],\pi_e^{u_j}[r']|r'\in[L]\}\). \(s_z:\langle\{w_i|v_i\in V\}\rangle,t_z:\langle\{\hat{u}_i|v_i\in V\}\rangle,\)
\(\hat{s}_z:\langle\{y_e|e\in E\}\rangle,\hat{t}_z:\langle\{x_e|e\in E\}\rangle,\)
\(u_i:\hat{w}_i\succ\langle\Theta(v_i)\rangle\succ w_i,w_i:u_i\succ s_1\succ\cdots\succ s_h,\)
\(\hat{u}_i:\hat{w}_i\succ t_1\succ\cdots\succ t_h,\hat{w}_i:\hat{u}_i\succ u_i,\)
\(x_e:y_e\succ\hat{t}_1\succ\cdots\succ\hat{t}_{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{h}{2}},y_e:x_e\succ\langle\Pi(e)\rangle\succ\hat{s}_1\succ\cdots\succ\hat{s}_{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{h}{2}},\)
\(\pi_e^{u_i}[r]:\theta_e^{u_i}[r]\succ y_e\succ\hat{\theta}_e^{u_i}[r],\theta_e^{u_i}[r]:\hat{\pi}_e^{u_i}[r]\succ u_i\succ\pi_e^{u_i}[r],\)
\(\hat{\pi}_e^{u_i}[r]:\hat{\theta}_e^{u_i}[r]\succ\theta_e^{u_i}[r],\hat{\theta}_e^{u_i}[r]:\pi_e^{u_i}[r]\succ\hat{\pi}_e^{u_i}[r],\)
\(\hat{\pi}_e^{u_j}[r]:\hat{\theta}_e^{u_j}[r]\succ\theta_e^{u_j}[r],\hat{\theta}_e^{u_j}[r]:\pi_e^{u_j}[r]\succ\hat{\pi}_e^{u_j}[r],\)
\(\pi_e^{u_j}[r]:\theta_e^{u_j}[r]\succ y_e\succ\hat{\theta}_e^{u_j}[r],\theta_e^{u_j}[r]:\hat{\pi}_e^{u_j}[r]\succ u_j\succ\pi_e^{u_j}[r].\)

To complete the construction, let _k_=|_U_|, meaning that we are aiming for a perfect matching with minimum number of blocking pairs. Let \(\beta=h+\genfrac(){pt}{2}{h}{2}\). The statement follows from the following claims.

**Claim 1.** _If G admits a clique of size h, then there exists a perfect matching with at most_ \(\beta\) _blocking pairs._

_Proof._ Let _K_ be a size-_h_ clique and let \(E'\) be the induced edges in _G_\[_K_\]. Without loss of generality, assume that _K_={_v_<sub>1</sub>_,...,v<sub>h</sub>_} and \(E'=\{e_1,\dots,e_{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{h}{2}}\}\). We construct a matching _M_ as follows.

(1) Match the agents in \(\{\hat{u}_1,\dots,\hat{u}_k\}\cup\{t_1,\dots,t_h\}\) according to a perfect stable matching of _I_ restricted to \(\{\hat{u}_1,\dots,\hat{u}_k\}\cup\{t_1,\dots,t_h\}\); since the acceptability graph of the restricted to these agents is complete, we can find such a matching in polynomial time with Gale-Shapley algorithm \[11\]. Do the same for the set \(\{s_1,\dots,s_k\}\cup\{w_1,\dots,w_k\}\). For every \(v_j\in K\), let \(M(u_j)=\hat{w}_j\).<tbc>

(2) For each vertex \(v_i\notin K\), let \(M(\hat{u}_i)=\hat{w}_i\), and _M(u<sub>i</sub>_)=_w<sub>i</sub>_.<tbc>

(3) Match the agents in \(\{\hat{t}_1,\dots,\hat{t}_{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{h}{2}}\}\cup\{x_1,\dots,x_{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{h}{2}}\}\) according to a perfect stable matching of _I_ restricted to \(\{\hat{t}_1,\dots,\hat{t}_{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{h}{2}}\}\cup\{x_1,\dots,x_{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{h}{2}}\}\); since the acceptability graph of the restricted to these agents is complete, we can find such a matching in polynomial time using the Gale-Shapley algorithm \[11\]. Do the same for the set \(\{\hat{s}_1,\dots,\hat{s}_{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{h}{2}}\}\cup\{y_1,\dots,y_{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{h}{2}}\}\). For each edge \(e_z\in E'\) and each incident vertex _v<sub>i</sub>_, and each \(r\in[L]\), let \(M(\pi_{e_z}^{u_i}[r])=\theta_{e_z}^{u_i}[r]\) and \(M(\hat{\pi}_{e_z}^{u_i}[r])=\hat{\theta}_{e_z}^{u_i}[r]\).<tbc>

(4) For each edge \(e\notin E'\) and each incident vertex _v<sub>i</sub>_, and each \(r\in[L]\), do the following. Let _M(x<sub>e</sub>_)=_y<sub>e</sub>_, \(M(\pi_e^{u_i}[r])=\hat{\theta}_e^{u_i}[r]\) and \(M(\hat{\pi}_e^{u_i}[r])=\theta_e^{u_i}[r]\).

It remains to show that _M_ induces at most \(\beta\) blocking pairs. Let us consider every agent from _U_.

- No vertex selector agent can be involved in a blocking pair since they only prefer a vertex agent with lower index, but _M_ restricted to the vertex selectors and vertex agents is stable by construction.<tbc>

- Similarly, no edge selector agent can be involved in a blocking pair.<tbc>

- Let \(v_i\notin K\) be an arbitrary non-clique vertex. Agent \(\hat{u}_i\) is already matched with his most preferred agent. Agent _u<sub>i</sub>_ prefers \(\hat{w}_i\) to his partner _w<sub>i</sub>_, but agent \(\hat{w}_i\) is matched with his most preferred agent; see (2). Agent _u<sub>i</sub>_ also prefers each agent \(\theta_e^{u_i}[r]\) to his partner _w<sub>i</sub>_. But each \(\theta_e^{u_i}[r]\) is matched with his most preferred agent \(\hat{\pi}_e^{u_i}[r]\) since no edge incident to _v<sub>i</sub>_ is in \(E'\); see (4).<tbc>

- Let \(e\notin E'\) be an arbitrary non-clique edge. Agent _x<sub>e</sub>_ is already matched with his most preferred agent _y<sub>e</sub>_.<tbc>

- Let \(e\notin E'\) be an arbitrary non-clique edge and let \(r\in[L],v_i\in e\). Agent \(\pi_e^{u_i}[r]\) prefers _y<sub>e</sub>_ to his partner, but agent _y<sub>e</sub>_ is already matched with his most preferred partner _x<sub>e</sub>_; see (4). Agent \(\pi_e^{u_i}[r]\) also prefers \(\theta_e^{u_i}[r]\) to his partner, but \(\theta_e^{u_i}[r]\) is already matched with his most preferred partner. Agent \(\hat{\pi}_e^{u_i}[r]\) prefers \(\hat{\theta}_e^{u_i}[r]\) to his partner, but \(\hat{\theta}_e^{u_i}[r]\) is already matched with his most preferred partner.<tbc>

- Let \(v_i\in K\) be an arbitrary clique vertex. Agent _u<sub>i</sub>_ is matched to his most preferred agent. Agent \(\hat{u}_i\) forms with \(\hat{w}_i\) a blocking pair. He does not form with any vertex selector agent a blocking pair by reasoning analogously the first case.<tbc>

- Let \(e\in E'\) be an arbitrary clique edge. Agent _x<sub>e</sub>_ forms with _y<sub>e</sub>_ a blocking pair. He does not form with any edge selector agent a blocking pair. For each incident vertex _v<sub>i</sub>_ of _e_ (i.e., \(v_i\in K\)) and each \(r\in[L]\), both edge agents \(\pi_e^{u_i}[r]\) and \(\hat{\pi}_e^{u_i}[r]\) are already matched with their most preferred agents, respectively. So they will not form with anyone a blocking pair.

Summarizing, all but the last two cases yield blocking pairs. The last two cases give _h_ and \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{h}{2}\) blocking pairs, respectively. Hence, \(\beta=h+\genfrac(){pt}{2}{h}{2}\), as desired. (end of Claim 3) \(\diamond\)

Before we continue with the backward direction, let us observe the following.

**Claim 2.** _Let M be a perfect matching of the reduced instance. Then, for each edge_ \(e\in E\)_, it holds that M(y<sub>e</sub>_)=_x<sub>e</sub> or_ \(M(y_e)=\hat{s}_z\) _for some_ \(z\in[\genfrac(){pt}{2}{h}{2}]\).

_Proof._ Since _M_ is perfect, by the preferences of the edge selectors, we know that there are exactly \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{h}{2}\) edge-agents from _U_ that are each matched with some edge selector \(\hat{t}_z\) from _W_. The remaining \(\hat{m}-\genfrac(){pt}{2}{h}{2}\) edge-agents _x<sub>e</sub>_ must be matched with their only available partner _y<sub>e</sub>_. This leaves \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{h}{2}\) edge-agents from _W_ that are to be matched with some edge selector agents from _U_, as desired. (end of Claim 2) \(\diamond\)

**Claim 3.** _If G does not admit a clique of size h, then every perfect matching induces at least_ \(L>F(\beta)\cdot\beta\) _blocking pairs._

_Proof._ We show the contra-positive. Let _M_ be a perfect matching of the reduced instance with at most _L_-1 blocking pairs. Define \(K=\{v_i|M(\hat{u}_i)=t_z\text{for some}z\in[h]\}\) and \(E'=\{e|M(y_e)\in\hat{s}_z\text{for some}z\in[\genfrac(){pt}{2}{h}{2}]\}\). We aim to show that \(E'\) induces a size-_h_ clique.

Clearly |_K_|=_h_ and \(|E'|=\genfrac(){pt}{2}{h}{2}\) since _M_ is a perfect matching.

Consider an arbitrary edge \(e\in E'\) and let _e_={_v<sub>i</sub>,v<sub>j</sub>_}. We claim that both _v<sub>i</sub>_ and _v<sub>j</sub>_ must be in _K_.

Towards a contradiction, suppose that one of the endpoints of _e_ is not in _K_, say \(v_i\notin K\). Then, by definition and by the preferences of _u<sub>i</sub>_ we infer \(M(\hat{u}_i)=\hat{w}_i\). By the acceptability graph over _u<sub>i</sub>_, we infer that either _M(u<sub>i</sub>_)=_w<sub>i</sub>_ or \(M(u_i)\in\Theta(v_i)\).

If _M(u<sub>i</sub>_)=_w<sub>i</sub>_, then for each \(z\in[L]\), either \(\{u_i,\pi_e^{u_i}[z]\}\) or \(\{y_e,\theta_e^{u_i}[z]\}\) is blocking, inducing at least _L_ blocking pairs, a contradiction.

If \(M(u_i)=\theta_{e^\prime}^{u_i}[r]\) for some \(e'\in E\) with \(v_i\in e'\) and \(r\in[L]\), then by the preferences of \(\hat{\pi}_{e^\prime}^{u_i}\) we infer that \(M(\hat{\pi}_{e^\prime}^{u_i})=\hat{\theta}_{e^\prime}^{u_i}\). Since both \(\theta_{e^\prime}^{u_i}\) and \(\hat{\theta}_{e^\prime}^{u_i}\) are not available, we infer that \(M(\hat{\pi}_{e^\prime}^{u_i})=y_{e^\prime}\), a contradiction to Claim 2.

We have just shown that for each edge \(e\in E'\) both endpoints must be in _K_. Since \(|E'|=\genfrac(){pt}{2}{h}{2}\), we infer that \(|K|\ge h\). Since |_K_|=_h_, we immediately obtain that _K_ induces a clique of size _h_. (end of Claim 3) \(\diamond\)

Since Clique is W\[1\]-hard, the theorem follows directly from Claims 1 and 3.

We proceed with the roommates setting. We show that the same inapproximability result from the marriage setting holds for roommates setting even if we do not set any bound of the size of the target matching. The idea is to adapt the reduction from Theorem 1 by adding a very large but _even_ number of agents for every original agent with preferences so that each original agent must be matched as desired in that reduction in order to avoid too many blocking pairs. Note that such adaption has become a standard technique for many reduction; see for instance the work by Abraham et al. \[1, Lemma 2\] and Chen et al. \[6, Construction 2\].

**Corollary 1.** _Let_ \(F:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{N}\) _be an arbitrary computable function. Given an instance_ \((\mathcal{P},k,\beta)\) _of_ Min-BP- SRI-dec _it is_ W\[1\]_-hard to distinguish between the following two cases:_

(_i)_ P _admits a k matching with at most_ \(\beta\) _blocking pairs._<tbc>

_(ii)_ _Every matching of_ P _has at least_ \(F(\beta)\cdot\beta\) _blocking pairs._

_Proof._ As mentioned above, we will modify the reduction from Theorem 1. Let (_G,h_) be an instance of Clique, and let (_I,k_) be the instance of Min-BP-SMI constructed in Theorem 1. Let \(\hat{V}\) be the set of agents in _I_. Note that the reduction in Theorem 1 does not work for Min-BP-SRI, because Min-BP-SRI does not require every agent to be matched. To fix this, we add a large set _S<sub>u</sub>_ of even number of agents for each original agent _u_ in \(\hat{V}\) and append _S<sub>u</sub>_ to the end of the preferences of _u_ to ensure that _u_ is matched in the same way as in the proof for Theorem 1. Let \(\hat{I}\) be the modified instance for Min-BP-SRI. Then,

(i) if _M_ is a matching of _I_ in which every agent in \(\hat{V}\) is matched to another agent in \(\hat{V}\), then there is a matching \(M'\) of \(\hat{I}\) that admits the same number of blocking pairs as _M_, and<tbc>

(ii) if \(M'\) is a matching of \(I'\) in which some agent in \(\hat{V}\) is not matched to another agent in \(\hat{V}\), then \(M'\) admits more than _F(h_) blocking pairs.

Thus, the corollary follows.

## 4 FPT-approximability of Max-SMTI

In this section, we complement the result by Marx and Schlotter \[24\] and show that Max-SMTI admits an FPT-AS with respect to the number \(\tau\) of agents with preferences containing ties. More precisely, we provide an FPT-algorithm (with respect to \(\tau\)) that for every approximation ratio \(\varepsilon\in[\frac{2}{3},1)\) outputs a stable matching with size at least \(\varepsilon\cdot\text{OPT}(I)\) where OPT(_I_) denotes the size of an maximum-size stable matching in _I_. Note that we do not need to consider approximation factor between 0 and \(\frac{2}{3}\) since there is a factor-\(\frac{2}{3}\) polynomial-time algorithm by Király \[19\] and McDermid \[25\]. The idea of our algorithm is to show that for each approximation ratio \(\varepsilon\), either the size of a largest matching is upper-bounded by a function in \((\tau,\varepsilon)\) or the approximated result by Király \[19\] and McDermid \[25\] is good enough. In the former case, we apply the kernelization algorithm by Adil et al. \[2\] to obtain an FPT-algorithm for our parameter \((\tau,\varepsilon)\).

**Theorem 2.** Max-SMTI _admits an_ FPT-AS _with respect to the number_ \(\tau\) _agents with ties._

_Proof._ Let _I_ be an instance of Max-SMTI, \(\tau\) be the number of agents with ties, and \(\varepsilon\in[0,1)\) the approximation ratio we desire. As mentioned before, by the results of Király \[19\] and McDermid \[25\], we can assume without loss of generality that \(\varepsilon\ge\frac{2}{3}\). Further, let _M_<sup>∗</sup> be a maximum-size matching of the acceptability graph for _I_. We first observe the following relation between every stable matching and the size of _M_<sup>∗</sup>.

**Claim 4.** _For every stable matching of I, we have that_ \(|M^*|\le|M|+\tau\).

_Proof._ Consider the symmetric difference \(M^*\Delta M\). Each connected component in the symmetric difference is either a path and a cycle. Every cycle and even-length path component matches the same number of agents in both _M_ and _M_<sup>∗</sup>. Thus every component where _M_<sup>∗</sup> matches more agents must be an odd-length path. Moreover, each of these components matches precisely one extra pair.

Assume, towards a contradiction, that there are more odd-length paths than agents with ties. Then there must be some odd-length path component where no agent has a tie in his preference list.

Let (_v_<sub>1</sub>_,...,v<sub>t</sub>_) be such a path, where _t_ is even. In _M_<sup>∗</sup>, the pairs {_a_<sub>1</sub>_,a_<sub>2</sub>}_,...,_{_a_<sub>_t_-1</sub>_,a<sub>t</sub>_} are matched, whereas in _M_, the pairs {_a_<sub>2</sub>_,a_<sub>3</sub>}_,...,_{_a_<sub>_t_-2</sub>_,a_<sub>_t_-1</sub>} are matched, and _a_<sub>1</sub>_,a<sub>t</sub>_ are unmatched. Since _M_ is stable, it cannot be blocked by {_a_<sub>1</sub>_,a_<sub>2</sub>}. As _a_<sub>1</sub> is unmatched in _M_, it must be that \(a_2:a_3\succ a_1\). Since _M_<sup>∗</sup> is stable, it cannot be blocked by {_a_<sub>2</sub>_,a_<sub>3</sub>}, and we must have that \(a_3:a_4\succ a_2\). By repeating this argument, we obtain that \(a_{t-1}:a_t\succ a_{t-2}\). But then {_a_<sub>_t_-1</sub>_,a<sub>t</sub>_} blocks _M_, a contradiction. (end of Claim 4) \(\diamond\)

Let _M_ be a stable matching with \(|M|\ge\frac{2}{3}|M^*|\). Note that we can find _M_ in polynomial time by using for instance the algorithm of McDermid \[25\]. We proceed in two cases:

**Case 1:** \(|M|<\frac{\varepsilon\cdot\tau}{1-\varepsilon}\) . Then, \(|M^*|\le\frac{3}{2}|M|<\frac{3\varepsilon\cdot\tau}{2(1-\varepsilon)}\) . Since Max-SMTI has a size-_O(k_<sup>2</sup>) problem kernel \[2\] where _k_ is the target size of a stable matching in the natural parameterization of Max-SMTI, and _k_ is bounded by |_M_<sup>∗</sup>|, we can solve _I_ exactly in FPT-time with respect to \(\tau+\varepsilon\). Adil et al. \[2\] also provide an FPT-algorithm with running time _k_<sup>_O(k_)</sup>+_n_<sup>_O_(1)</sup>. Applying it, we obtain our FPT-algorithm with running time \(\frac{3\varepsilon\cdot\tau}{2(1-\varepsilon)}^{O(\frac{3\varepsilon\cdot\tau}{2(1-\varepsilon)})}+|I|^{O(1)}\).

**Case 2:** \(|M|\ge\frac{\varepsilon\cdot\tau}{1-\varepsilon}\) . Combining with Claim 4, \(|M^*|\le|M|+\frac{(1-\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon}\cdot|M|=\frac{|M|}{\varepsilon}\) . Thus, |_M_| is an \(\varepsilon\)- approximation.

As both cases lead to a \(\varepsilon\)-approximation in FPT-time, this concludes the proof.

## 5 Conclusion

In this manuscript, we have explored the fixed-parameter approximability of three problems in the field of stable matchings. Our goal is to highlight the potential of fixed-parameter approximability in the field of matching under preferences and computational social choice more generally. This technique can be used to solve problems that resist both polynomial-time approximation and FPT-algorithms. Using this technique more widely in the field of matchings and computational social choice is an open question. Of course, as we have in Theorem 1 and Corollary 1, some problems resist even this. Finding suitable parameters is part of the challenge.
